dataset_name: healthyIndia Curated and Verified Food Additive Reference
license: Open Reference Dataset for Consumer Transparency
disclaimer: Regulatory permissions under FSSAI are strictly category-specific according to the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011. The presence of an INS number does NOT indicate blanket permission across all food categories. Status is 'unverified' where category-specific authorization has not been audited. Identification of an additive indicates its technological presence and functional purpose; it does not evaluate personal medical risk or determine absolute food safety.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 142-47-2 | Molecular Formula: C5H8NO4Na | Monosodium salt of L-glutamic acid
additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI 'not specified' (allocated by JECFA in 1987 to substances of very low toxicity where total dietary intake does not represent a hazard to health)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Extensive double-blind placebo-controlled challenge studies (Geha et al., 2000; JECFA, 1987) demonstrated no consistent or reproducible causal relationship between dietary MSG intake and acute adverse symptoms in the general population. Transient symptoms (flushing, numbness, mild headache) have been documented in a small subset of sensitive individuals only after large oral bolus doses (>3g) administered without food. Oral dietary glutamate does not cross the intact adult blood-brain barrier in significant amounts.
additives.population_sensitivities: Prohibited in foods manufactured for infants below 12 months under Indian regulations. Sensitive individuals reporting sensitivity should monitor high-dose culinary seasonings.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 - Appendix A (GMP Table) & Regulation 3.1.11
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Authorizes monosodium glutamate under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) in specified food categories (seasonings, snacks, processed noodles). Strictly prohibits addition of MSG to any food meant for infants below 12 months.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 - Mandatory Declarations
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Legally mandates the label advisory 'NOT RECOMMENDED FOR INFANTS BELOW 12 MONTHS' whenever MSG is added to a food product.

sources.title: WHO / FAO JECFA Toxicological Evaluation of Certain Food Additives - Monosodium L-glutamate
sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.section_or_regulation: WHO Technical Report Series 759 (31st Report), Monograph 2464
sources.supported_claims: Allocated ADI 'not specified', concluding that dietary exposure to glutamate does not represent a toxicological hazard.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) in specified processed food categories under FSSAI regulations; strictly prohibited in foods intended for infants below 12 months. Mandatory statutory advisory required on label.
additives.scope_limitations: Permission is restricted to specific processed food categories; not authorized in milk, plain infant formula, or unflavoured staple commodities.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 22839-47-0 | Molecular Formula: C14H18N2O5 | N-L-alpha-Aspartyl-L-phenylalanine 1-methyl ester
additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI: 0–40 mg/kg body weight (established by JECFA in 1981, reaffirmed in July 2023)
additives.health_effects_evidence: In July 2023, WHO IARC classified aspartame as Group 2B ('possibly carcinogenic to humans' based on limited evidence in humans for hepatocellular carcinoma), while the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) reaffirmed that current intake levels are safe and maintained the ADI at 0–40 mg/kg bw, finding no convincing evidence of adverse effects within this limit. An adult weighing 60 kg would need to consume 12–36 cans of diet soda containing 200–300 mg aspartame daily to exceed the ADI, assuming no other dietary sources.
additives.population_sensitivities: Severe metabolic hazard for individuals suffering from Phenylketonuria (PKU), who lack the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase needed to metabolize phenylalanine. Requires prominent statutory packaging warning.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 - Table 2 (Artificial Sweeteners)
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Authorizes aspartame only in specified food categories subject to strict statutory numerical limits (e.g. carbonated water max 700 ppm, chewing gum max 10,000 ppm, confectionery max 2,000 ppm). Prohibited in general foods outside authorized list.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 - Artificial Sweetener Declarations
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Mandates explicit label disclosures: 'CONTAINS ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER' and 'NOT RECOMMENDED FOR PHENYLKETONURICS' along with the quantity of sweetener.

sources.title: WHO IARC & JECFA Joint Assessment of Aspartame (2023)
sources.organization: World Health Organization (WHO) & JECFA
sources.section_or_regulation: WHO Summary Report & JECFA 96th Meeting Findings
sources.supported_claims: IARC classified aspartame as Group 2B (possible carcinogen, limited evidence); JECFA reaffirmed safety at intake within the established ADI of 0-40 mg/kg body weight.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted only in specified food categories subject to quantitative maximum limits. Mandatory statutory warnings required on packaging: 'CONTAINS ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER' and 'NOT RECOMMENDED FOR PHENYLKETONURICS'.
additives.scope_limitations: Prohibited in general foods outside explicitly authorized product categories.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 8028-89-5 | Complex polymeric colouring material prepared by controlled heat treatment of carbohydrates with ammonium and sulfite compounds
additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI: 0–200 mg/kg body weight (established by JECFA in 1985 on solids basis, reaffirmed in 2000)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Toxicological evaluations focus on 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI), a trace processing byproduct formed during ammonia caramel manufacturing. High doses of isolated 4-MEI in animal bioassays produced alveolar/bronchiolar neoplasms in mice. JECFA, EFSA, and FSSAI established strict statutory purity specifications limiting 4-MEI to maximum 250 mg/kg in commercial Caramel IV (on equivalent colour basis). At regulatory purity standards, human dietary exposure to 4-MEI is negligible and toxicologically safe within the ADI.
additives.population_sensitivities: May contain trace bound sulfur dioxide/sulfites from the manufacturing process. Individuals diagnosed with severe sulfite hypersensitivity should check product allergen statements.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 - Regulation 3.1.4 (Food Colours)
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Permits Caramel IV in specified food categories (carbonated beverages, confectionery, baked goods, sauces) subject to purity specifications including max 250 mg/kg 4-MEI limit.

sources.title: JECFA Toxicological Evaluation of Certain Food Additives - Caramel Colours
sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.supported_claims: Allocated group ADI of 0-200 mg/kg bw for Caramel IV on solids basis; concluded dietary exposure within purity standards presents no carcinogenic risk.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted in specified food categories (including carbonated beverages, confectionery, baked goods) subject to statutory limits and purity specifications (including 4-MEI threshold).
additives.scope_limitations: Prohibited in fresh meat, fruit juices, tea, coffee, and unflavoured dairy products.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 8002-43-5 | Complex mixture of polar phosphatides (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidic acid)
additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI 'not limited' / 'not specified' (established by JECFA in 1973)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Lecithins are naturally occurring structural lipids found in egg yolk, soybeans, sunflower seeds, and all animal and plant cell membranes. Metabolized as normal dietary fats into choline, fatty acids, and glycerol. Non-toxic at all dietary exposure levels.
additives.population_sensitivities: When derived from soybeans (common in commercial packaged foods), traces of residual soy protein can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with severe IgE-mediated soya allergy. FSSAI mandates explicit declaration of the botanical allergen source.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 - Appendix A
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Permits lecithins under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) across general food formulations.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 - Allergen Labelling
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Requires mandatory declaration of botanical allergen source (e.g. Soya) when an additive is derived from recognized allergen commodities.

sources.title: JECFA Toxicological Evaluation of Certain Food Additives - Lecithins
sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.supported_claims: Assigned ADI 'not limited', recognizing physiological lipid nature with no toxicological risk.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) across processed food formulations. Botanical allergen source (e.g. Soya) must be disclosed on packaging.
additives.scope_limitations: Authorized for GMP usage; subject to mandatory allergen disclosure if soy-derived.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 532-32-1 | Molecular Formula: C7H5NaO2 | Sodium salt of benzenecarboxylic acid
additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI: 0–5 mg/kg body weight (established by JECFA in 1996, expressed as benzoic acid equivalent)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Sodium benzoate is absorbed and rapidly conjugated with glycine in the liver to form hippuric acid, which is excreted in urine within 24 hours. In acidic beverages formulated with both sodium benzoate and ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), trace catalytic decarboxylation can form benzene under heat and UV exposure. Strict manufacturing controls, pH management, and statutory surveillance ensure benzene formation remains well below the WHO drinking water guideline of 10 ppb (0.01 mg/L). Non-toxic at permitted statutory concentrations.
additives.population_sensitivities: Non-immunological pseudo-allergic reactions (urticaria, contact dermatitis, asthma exacerbation) have been reported in a small fraction of individuals with pre-existing aspirin-sensitive asthma or chronic idiopathic urticaria.

sources.title: WHO / FAO JECFA Toxicological Evaluation of Certain Food Additives - Benzoates
sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.supported_claims: Established group ADI of 0-5 mg/kg body weight for benzoic acid and its sodium, potassium, and calcium salts.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted Class II chemical preservative with strict statutory numerical limits by food category. Prohibited in foods where chemical preservation is disallowed.
additives.scope_limitations: Strict category-specific maximum residue limits apply; prohibited in foods where chemical preservation is disallowed.

additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI 'not limited' / 'not specified' (established by JECFA in 1973)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Citric acid is a fundamental intermediate in the citric acid (Krebs) cycle of cellular metabolism in all aerobic organisms. It is completely metabolized into carbon dioxide and water; non-toxic at all dietary intake levels. Frequent, prolonged dietary contact with high-concentration acidic beverages can promote dental enamel demineralization (erosion).
additives.population_sensitivities: No recognized dietary allergy. Concentrated solutions can cause transient local oral mucosal irritation.

sources.title: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 - Appendix A
sources.organization: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
sources.supported_claims: Permits citric acid under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) across virtually all processed food categories unless prohibited by a specific commodity standard.

sources.title: JECFA Toxicological Evaluation of Certain Food Additives - Citric Acid
sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.supported_claims: Allocated ADI 'not limited', recognizing essential role in cellular energy metabolism.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) in most processed food categories unless prohibited by a specific commodity standard.
additives.scope_limitations: GMP usage across broad food categories.

additives.acceptable_daily_intake: ADI: 0–10 mg/kg body weight (established by JECFA in 2016, increased from earlier 0-7.5 mg/kg bw based on comprehensive multigenerational reproductive and neurobehavioral studies)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Comprehensive toxicological evaluations by JECFA (2016), EFSA (2009), and US FDA found no evidence of genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, or neurotoxicity in animal bioassays at dietary exposure levels. A small proportion (<0.1%) of the population, predominantly individuals with known aspirin-induced asthma, exhibits clinical pseudo-allergic cross-reactivity (urticaria, rhinitis, bronchospasm). The 2007 Southampton study observed slight increases in hyperactivity in children consuming a mixture of synthetic colours and sodium benzoate, but JECFA and EFSA concluded the evidence does not establish a causal neurological relationship for the general population.
additives.population_sensitivities: Cross-sensitivity in patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma or chronic idiopathic urticaria. Mandatory bold statutory packaging disclosure required in India.

sources.organization: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
sources.supported_claims: Established ADI of 0-10 mg/kg body weight based on no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) of 984 mg/kg bw/day.

additives.regulatory_status: Permitted synthetic food colour strictly limited to authorized categories with mandatory upper limits (max 100 ppm; max 200 ppm in canned fruit). Requires mandatory label disclosure: 'CONTAINS PERMITTED SYNTHETIC FOOD COLOUR(S)'.
additives.scope_limitations: Strict authorized category list; strictly prohibited in unprocessed staples, dairy products, tea, and infant foods.

additives.chemical_identity: CAS 144-55-8 | Molecular Formula: NaHCO3 | Monosodium salt of carbonic acid (commonly known as baking soda / sodium bicarbonate)
additives.health_effects_evidence: Completely dissociates into sodium (Na+) and bicarbonate (HCO3-) ions in the gastrointestinal tract, reacting with gastric acid to release carbon dioxide gas and water. Both ions are homeostatically regulated in human physiology. Non-toxic. Contributes to total dietary sodium intake (27.4% sodium by weight).
additives.population_sensitivities: Individuals placed on severe therapeutic sodium-restricted diets (e.g. for congestive heart failure or severe hypertension) should account for sodium contributed by chemical leaveners.
